nj_allamuchy_mountain_sp_boulders.blurb: Scattered granite boulders in a talus field among the woods of Allamuchy Mountain State Park, in northwest New Jersey. The problems are mostly easy to moderate, with plenty of V0 to V3 and a handful of harder lines up toward V7, and some of the boulders are tall for their grade. The granite is coarse and can be crumbly in spots, and summer growth means brushing holds and cleaning top-outs. Much of the fun is wandering off the trails to find lines visible through the trees. Fall through early spring is the comfortable stretch; summer is humid and buggy. Black bears and deer are around, and wear bright clothing during hunting season.
nj_allamuchy_mountain_sp_boulders.parking_note: Use the dirt lot next to the Scout Reservation entrance on Waterloo Road (County Route 604). The teal-blazed trail from there leads up into most of the bouldering.
nj_allamuchy_mountain_sp_boulders.approach: From the lot, follow the teal-blazed trail uphill into the talus; a few of the nearer boulders sit a couple of hundred yards off the trail, and the rest are found by exploring the stream bed and ridge sides.

nm_main_wall_4.blurb: The big west-facing wall at The Shack, a sport crag tucked onto the back side of Diablo Mesa near the Rio Grande gorge north of Santa Fe. It is the first wall you meet on the walk in and holds most of the routes at the crag. Nearly everything is bolted, and the grades cluster around 5.11 and 5.12, with a few easier lines and a couple of 5.13s for the strong. The crag is shaded through the morning, which makes it a good pick in the warm seasons, though in summer the sun reaches the wall by late morning. Watch for rattlesnakes on the approach, and bring a stick-clip if you like one for the first bolts.
nm_main_wall_4.parking_note: Keep going beyond Diablo's main lot to a pullout near the pump station on the left; park across the road from it rather than in front. Sand berms along the road have stranded 2WD trucks, so AWD or 4WD is wise.
nm_main_wall_4.approach: The crag cannot be seen from the road. A trail starts across the arroyo, climbs a gully and traverses to the nose of a ridge set apart from the main cliff band; the wall appears as you arrive near a large detached pinnacle.

nm_main_cliff.blurb: The tallest and longest-lined cliff in Capulin Canyon, a remote crack-climbing canyon in the Dome Wilderness of the Jemez Mountains. The rock is welded volcanic tuff that takes gear well, and the climbing is all traditional, with no sport routes. Most lines fall in the 5.10 and 5.11 range and some run up to a rope length, so two ropes are handy. Expect loose rock and dirt in places, and note that many routes see few ascents, so tap holds and wear a helmet. The cliffs are cooler in spring and fall, and the walk in drops steeply into the canyon and climbs back out at day's end.
nm_main_cliff.approach: Take the main trail from the parking area to the dry wash, follow the wash downstream, then leave it at a cairn on your left and climb the marked path up to the cliff.

nm_upper_wall.blurb: The most varied wall in Capulin Canyon, a remote trad area in the Dome Wilderness of the Jemez Mountains. Routes here are dense and mixed in character, with splitter cracks and corners in welded volcanic tuff that holds gear well. Grades are mostly 5.10 and 5.11, with a few 5.9s and several 5.12s. Everything is traditional or top-rope; there are no sport lines. The rock firms and softens unevenly from bottom to top and loose pieces turn up on cracks, so tap holds and wear a helmet. Walls in the canyon face mostly south and get strong sun, so spring and fall are the comfortable seasons, and summer is very hot.

nm_pizza_boulders.blurb: A bouldering area on the western slope of the Dona Ana Mountains, north of Las Cruces and across from the Checkerboard Wall. The problems are old-school and aesthetic, with a wide spread from V0 into the double digits and the bulk of them in the V2 to V5 range. Holds can be sparse and spacing demanding, so shorter climbers may find grades stiff. Many problems face north, which stretches the season into warmer months compared with other Las Cruces boulders. Getting in takes an off-road capable vehicle, trails are overgrown, and snakes are common in the desert. Cell service is spotty, so tell someone your plan. Pack out all trash and treat old bolts on the big blocks with caution.

ny_moss_island_climbs.blurb: The climbing on Moss Island, a small island in the Mohawk River at Little Falls, a popular outdoor gym for central New York. The main cliff runs along the south side, roughly 30 to 40 feet high, with slabs, vertical faces and steep overhangs. Most routes are set up for top-roping from anchors that sit well back from the edge, so bring long slings or webbing; only a handful take good gear for leading. Grades run from very easy up past 5.12, with the bulk between 5.7 and 5.10. Some boulder problems sit on the cooler north side. The south-facing cliff bakes on sunny summer days, so spring and fall are more pleasant.

ny_panther_gorge.blurb: A wild cirque between Mount Marcy and Haystack in the Adirondack High Peaks, with cliffs of anorthosite roughly 200 to 400 feet tall. It is one of the most remote crags in the East, reached by a long hike and a bushwhack through dense spruce. The rock climbing is traditional, mostly in the 5.7 to 5.9 range on cracks, chimneys, slabs and arêtes, with multi-pitch lines on the larger faces. Cracks can be dirty and sharp, so tape and long pants help. In winter there are moderate ice and mixed routes, mostly WI3 to WI5. The season is short: black flies are bad in early summer, some rock stays wet into August, and ice can start forming in October. Carry a full rack, double ropes, a helmet and a bear canister.
ny_panther_gorge.approach: A long backcountry trek of roughly eight miles from the trailhead, then a short bushwhack through dense spruce to the base of the cliffs. Many parties camp in or near the gorge rather than do it in a day.

ny_sleepy_hollow.blurb: The scattered routes and small crags at the far end of the Trapps, the longest and busiest cliff in the Gunks. The rock is the Gunks' quartz conglomerate, with horizontal cracks, roofs and jugs, and the roped climbing is traditional, mostly one to three pitches with a broad spread from easy to hard. A smaller set of boulder problems sits here too, ranging up to V9. The Trapps draws big crowds on spring and fall weekends, and parking lots fill early on fine days. September and October are the prime months, summer is hot and humid, and spring can be wetter and buggier. Gunks ratings run stiff, so expect a hard feel for the grade.

_conflicts.nm_main_wall_4: rock: stored sandstone, sources say basalt (https://blm.gov/visit/diablo-canyon, https://advcollective.com/united_states/Climbing/climb-at-diablo-canyon-near-santa-fe)
_conflicts.nm_pizza_boulders: rock: stored volcanic rock, Mountain Project describes the Dona Ana Mountains as granitic (https://www.mountainproject.com/area/106603617/las-cruces-area-climbing)
_conflicts.ny_moss_island_climbs: rock: stored gneiss, Wikipedia says metasyenite and Mountain Project says gneiss vs black granite is unsettled (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moss_Island, https://www.mountainproject.com/area/105830357/moss-island)
